edits.html:
Kawasaki Disease

Medium-vessel vasculitis · a 10-day clock · fever for 5 days plus 4 criteria: treat now?

ScriptStem cuesDiagnosisManagementPreventionComplicationsPractice
Bottom line

Diagnosis is clinical: fever for 5 days or more plus at least 4 of 5 CRASH criteria. IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin) must be given within 10 days of fever onset, with aspirin, and an echocardiogram is obtained at diagnosis. Treat now; do not delay it for a workup. Sterile pyuria is a feature of Kawasaki disease. Kawasaki disease causes urethritis, giving urinary white blood cells with no bacteria.

Exception: with only 2 or 3 criteria (incomplete disease, especially in infants under 6 months), use CRP (C-reactive protein) and ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate), supplemental labs and echocardiography, and treat if they are supportive.

Illness script
Kawasaki disease
What it isMedium-vessel vasculitis that targets the coronary arteries
DriverImmune-mediated arteritis; the cause is unknown
TriggersNone proven; age under 5 and Asian ancestry, especially Japanese, raise risk (non-modifiable)
WhoYoung children; infants under 6 months have the most atypical presentations
LooksFever for 5 days or more with the CRASH findings; irritable
LabsAnemia, low albumin, high ALT (alanine aminotransferase), sterile pyuria; platelets high after day 7
CourseUntreated, coronary aneurysm risk is ~20–25%; IVIG within 10 days lowers it to ~3–5%
Chain: Kawasaki disease

Vasculitis

→ an immune response inflames medium-sized arteries

→ the coronary arteries are the main target

Structural

→ the inflamed coronary wall dilates into an aneurysm

→ the aneurysm can expand, rupture or clot

Clinical

→ myocardial ischemia or infarction

→ heart failure: fast breathing, fast pulse, low blood pressure, big heart

How it hides in a stem
History and examination: what each clue points to
ClueWhat it points to
Fever for 5 days or moreBurn: the gate; then count the criteria
"Pink eye"Nonexudative conjunctivitis: a criterion; pus points to adenovirus
Strawberry tongue, cracked red lipsOral criterion; ulcers point to Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Red swollen hands; later, peeling at the nailsExtremity criterion; the peeling comes in week 2 to 3
A single neck node 1.5 cm or largerAdenopathy, the least common criterion
Past high fever, red eyes, swollen red hands, big nodes, cracked lipsAn earlier Kawasaki illness: fever plus 4 criteria
That illness cleared on its own within 14 daysUntreated: no IVIG, so the coronary risk remained
The illness was 2 months beforeTime for aneurysms to cause heart failure ⚠︎ (role inferred)
A boy of 18 monthsThe usual age: most cases are under 5 ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Brought to the emergency department; 2 days of increasingly rapid breathing, irritableAn acute presentation; the symptom asked about: heart or lung? ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Now in obvious discomfortAn ill child; fits low cardiac output ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Vital signs, tests and pertinent negatives: what each clue points to
ClueWhat it points to
Temperature 38 C (100.4 F) two months laterLow grade: an ill child, not a new Kawasaki fever ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Pulse 150/min, respirations 60/minTachycardia, tachypnea: heart failure; tamponade shares them ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Blood pressure 60/40 mm HgHypotension: low output; tamponade also lowers it ⚠︎ (role inferred)
No other abnormal finding on examinationNo murmur: argues against mitral obstruction; no jugular distension or pulsus paradoxus argues against tamponade
Cardiomegaly on the chest x-rayA big heart; interstitial lung disease would show fibrosis
ST-segment depression in leads II and IIIIschemia from coronary disease ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Left ventricular hypertrophy, right-axis deviationVentricular strain in a failing heart ⚠︎ (role inferred)
White cells in the urine, no bacteriaSterile pyuria: part of Kawasaki disease, not a UTI (urinary tract infection)
Weeks after COVID-19, vomiting, low blood pressureMIS-C (multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children), not Kawasaki disease
Diagnosis
Diagnostic criteria Kawasaki disease – fever for 5 days or more plus at least 4 of 5 CRASH criteria · Incomplete disease – fever for 5 days or more with only 2–3 criteria · Evaluate for incomplete disease – an infant 6 months or younger with fever for 7 days or more and no other explanation · IVIG resistance – fever persisting 36 h after IVIG
CRASH and Burn
  • Conjunctivitis – bilateral, nonexudative, limbal sparing
  • Rash – polymorphous, perineal accentuation with desquamation
  • Adenopathy – cervical ≥1.5 cm, usually unilateral (the least common criterion)
  • Strawberry tongue / cracked red lips – no ulcers, no exudate
  • Hands and feet – erythema and edema acutely, periungual desquamation in week 2–3
  • Burn – fever ≥5 days
First tests
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
CRP and ESRFirstElevatedSupports Kawasaki
EchocardiogramFirstCoronary dilation or aneurysmBaseline at diagnosis; in suspected incomplete disease, coronary changes justify IVIG
CBC (complete blood count), albumin, ALT and urinalysisBy branchAnemia, low albumin, high ALT, sterile pyuria; platelets high after day 7Supportive labs for incomplete Kawasaki; in incomplete disease, a raised CRP or ESR triggers supplemental labs and echo
Rapid strep testBy branchPositive, with sandpaper rash and no conjunctivitisScarlet fever: penicillin
None: clinical diagnosisConfirmsFever 5 days or more plus 4 of 5 criteriaTests support and stage it; IVIG within 10 days is not delayed for them
Urine culture for the pyuriaSkipSterile pyuria is part of KawasakiUrethritis from the disease; do not hold IVIG for a UTI workup
Kawasaki mimics and their discriminators
DiagnosisThe stem showsDecides itConfirms
AdenovirusFever, red eyes, sore throatExudative conjunctivitis and pharyngitis; Kawasaki's is nonexudativeViral testing of a throat or eye swab
Scarlet feverFever, strawberry tongue, responds to penicillinSandpaper rash, Pastia lines, no conjunctivitisRapid strep test; throat culture if negative
MeaslesCough/coryza, unvaccinatedKoplik spots, cephalocaudal rashMeasles antibody serology or viral testing
MIS-CPost-COVID, older children, prominent GI symptomsShockClinical criteria plus a positive COVID-19 test or antibodies
Toxic shock syndromeFever, rash, desquamation laterHypotension + multiorgan failureClinical criteria; negative cultures
Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysisTarget lesions, drug exposureMucosal erosions and ulcersClinical; skin biopsy
Staphylococcal scalded skinPerioral crustingNikolsky positiveClinical
Management and treatment
Management ladder
TierInterventionEscalate when
Diagnosis madeIVIG 2 g/kg plus high-dose aspirin, within 10 days of fever onsetFever persisting 36 h after IVIG
Seen after day 10IVIG if unexplained fever or coronary changes persist with a raised CRP or ESRFever persisting 36 h after IVIG
IVIG resistanceSecond IVIG dose; steroids or infliximab as alternativesTop rung

Step down: high-dose aspirin acutely, then low-dose once afebrile for 48 to 72 hours (practice varies). Kawasaki is the exception to the rule against aspirin in children.

Follow-up and return precautions Echocardiogram – at diagnosis, then 1 to 2 weeks and 4 to 6 weeks after treatment in uncomplicated disease ⚠︎ (a 2024 guideline update may shorten the first recheck; unverified) · Return – fast breathing or irritability weeks later needs an ECG (electrocardiogram) and echocardiogram
Distractors
Salient decoyUrine culture and antibiotics: pyuria looks like a UTI; it is sterile and part of the disease.
Sequencing trapWaiting for a fourth criterion: coronary changes on the echocardiogram already justify IVIG.
Unchecked attributeNo IVIG after day 10: the 10-day mark is a target, not a cutoff; with persistent unexplained fever or coronary changes and a raised CRP or ESR, IVIG is still reasonable.
True-fact-wrong-slotAvoiding aspirin in a child: the Reye rule is real, but Kawasaki is the exception.
Prevention and screening
  • No vaccine or drug prevents Kawasaki disease; IVIG within 10 days prevents most aneurysms.
  • Live vaccines: MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) and varicella must be deferred 11 months after IVIG.
Complications and long-term sequelae
  • Coronary aneurysm: can expand, rupture or cause a myocardial infarction; infants under 6 months have the highest aneurysm risk.
  • Heart failure: tachypnea, tachycardia, hypotension, cardiomegaly and ischemic ST depression.
  • Pericardial effusion: a real complication; tamponade adds raised jugular venous pressure and pulsus paradoxus.
  • Mitral valve: regurgitation, not stenosis.
  • Lungs and pulmonary vessels: rarely involved.
  • Workup: ECG and echocardiogram as soon as Kawasaki is suspected.
Practice
  1. 18-month-old boy brought to the emergency department with 2 days of increasingly fast breathing and irritability; 2 months earlier he had a high fever, red eyes, cracked red lips, enlarged lymph nodes and red swollen hands, all of which cleared without treatment within 14 days; in obvious discomfort; T 38 C (100.4 F); HR 150/min; RR 60/min; BP 60/40 mm Hg; the rest of the examination is normal; chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly; ECG: ST-segment depression in leads II and III, left ventricular hypertrophy, right-axis deviation → Congestive heart failure → late cardiac complication of untreated Kawasaki disease: cardiomegaly with ischemic ST depression, and no murmur or signs of tamponade
  2. 4-year-old boy with 6 days of fever; T 39.5 C; bilateral conjunctivitis without discharge; strawberry tongue; a polymorphous rash; edema of both hands; one cervical lymph node 1.8 cm → Kawasaki disease → fever 5 days or more plus at least 4 of 5 criteria; IVIG plus aspirin
  3. 4-year-old boy with 5 days of fever; T 39.0 C; only 3 of the 5 criteria are present: bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips and a polymorphous rash; echocardiogram shows coronary artery dilation → IVIG and aspirin now → incomplete Kawasaki disease is treated on the coronary finding
  4. 4-year-old boy brought in on day 12 of fever; T 39.1 C; bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, a polymorphous rash and swollen red hands since the first week; CRP 12 mg/dL → IVIG now → give IVIG even beyond day 10 when unexplained fever or coronary changes persist with a raised CRP or ESR
  5. 4-year-old boy with 2 days of fever and sore throat; T 39.4 C; exudative pharyngitis; strawberry tongue; a fine sandpaper-like rash, densest in the skin creases; no conjunctivitis → Scarlet fever → a positive rapid strep test confirms it; penicillin
  6. 4-year-old boy who is unvaccinated; 4 days of fever, cough and runny nose; T 39.8 C; bilateral conjunctivitis; Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa; a red rash that began on the face and is spreading downward → Measles → Koplik spots and a descending rash decide it; measles antibody serology confirms
  7. 4-year-old boy with 6 days of fever; T 39.1 C; bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, a polymorphous rash and swollen hands; IVIG and aspirin are ordered; urinalysis shows many white blood cells and no bacteria → Continue IVIG and aspirin as planned → sterile pyuria is Kawasaki urethritis, a feature of the disease, not a second diagnosis
  8. 9-year-old boy with 3 days of fever, abdominal pain and vomiting, 4 weeks after COVID-19; T 39.5 C; HR 168/min; BP 70/40 mm Hg; a diffuse red rash; cool hands and feet; creatinine 1.3 mg/dL; troponin raised → Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children → weeks after COVID-19, with prominent GI symptoms and shock
  9. 3-year-old boy with 6 days of fever; T 39.4 C; bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, a polymorphous rash and swollen red hands → Echocardiogram → baseline coronary assessment at diagnosis; IVIG is not delayed for it
  10. 2-year-old girl, 3 weeks after 7 days of fever with conjunctivitis, cracked lips, rash and hand swelling that were never treated; afebrile now; peeling skin around the fingernails; platelet count 780,000/mm³ → Coronary artery aneurysm → echocardiogram now; untreated aneurysms can progress to infarction or heart failure
  11. 5-year-old girl who received IVIG 2 g/kg and high-dose aspirin for Kawasaki disease; the infusion ended 40 hours ago; T 39.3 C; conjunctivitis and rash persist → Second dose of IVIG → fever persisting 36 h after IVIG defines resistance
  12. 3-year-old boy at a well visit 2 months after he was given IVIG 2 g/kg for Kawasaki disease; afebrile; aspirin stopped after a normal echocardiogram; due for routine vaccines → Measles-mumps-rubella and varicella vaccines today → live vaccines are deferred 11 months after IVIG; inactivated vaccines are not
  13. 6-year-old boy treated with IVIG and aspirin for Kawasaki disease; afebrile since the day after the infusion; echocardiogram at diagnosis normal → Repeat echocardiogram at 1 to 2 weeks and 4 to 6 weeks → coronary changes can appear after a normal first study
How NBME framed it The untreated Kawasaki illness sits in the past history as an episode that resolved on its own, and the mechanism lead-in is keyed to heart failure. The criteria appear in lay words ("pink eye," swollen hands) and are never named.
Distractors: NBME question
True-fact-wrong-slotPericardial effusion: a real Kawasaki complication, but tamponade adds raised jugular venous pressure and pulsus paradoxus; cardiomegaly with ischemic ST depression fits heart failure.
Unchecked attributeMitral valve obstruction: Kawasaki affects the mitral valve as regurgitation, not stenosis, and no stenotic murmur is heard.
Salient decoyChronic inflammatory interstitial lung disease: Kawasaki rarely involves the lungs, and the film shows cardiomegaly rather than interstitial fibrosis.
Class-vs-memberThickened internal layer of pulmonary arterioles: Kawasaki is a medium-vessel vasculitis that targets the coronary arteries and rarely involves the pulmonary vessels.
Pairs with Part I New Heart Failure in a Child: is the failing heart from an untreated Kawasaki illness in the history or from an acute viral myocarditis?
Transferable rules

A candidate diagnosis that explains only a subset of the findings is wrong. A UTI (urinary tract infection) explains two of the findings; Kawasaki explains all of them. Check which findings a diagnosis leaves unexplained.
